title: The Sharpe Pint: Strait Talking, Capital Cycles, and the Five Sins of Financial AI

opening_mood.text: Morning. If you spent the weekend enjoying the rare British sunshine, we have some bad news: geopolitics has crashed the party. The Strait of Hormuz is flaring up, oil is jumping, and the markets are nursing a proper Monday morning hangover. Grab a strong coffee as we unpack easyJet's bidding war, the real way to measure AI portfolio performance, and why almost every financial LLM paper you read is committing some cardinal sins.

content.text: 1. The Strait of Hormuz Flare-up: US-Iran Strikes Send Oil Jumping

Over the weekend and into Monday morning, the US launched several waves of airstrikes on Iran following an Iranian attack on a container ship in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran retaliated, and Brent crude immediately jumped by as much as 5% in early trading before settling back to around $77.72 per barrel. Just when markets thought a fragile interim ceasefire agreement was holding, this fresh escalation has thrown a spanner in the works, reminding everyone of the geopolitical risk premium that sits permanently under energy markets.

For anyone in macro or asset management, this is the ultimate wildcard. Rising oil prices quickly feed into transportation costs and manufacturing, threatening to reignite the inflation dragon just as central banks were preparing to ease off the brake. If the Strait of Hormuz remains contested, the Bank of England and the Federal Reserve will find their rate-cut timetables severely disrupted.

items: What to say at work: Just as we thought the Middle East risk premium was fading, the Strait of Hormuz reminds us why macro traders never sleep. If this escalates, expect the 'higher-for-longer' rate narrative to make a swift comeback, putting pressure on long-duration equities.

Interview tip: Be prepared to discuss how geopolitical supply shocks affect different asset classes—specifically, how rising oil prices act as a tax on consumers while boosting energy sector earnings.

content.text: 2. The Battle for easyJet: Apollo Gatecrashes with a £5.7bn Bid

US private equity giant Apollo Global Management has gatecrashed the sale of easyJet with a surprise £5.7bn (£7.15 per share) cash offer, triggering a proper bidding war. The easyJet board has swiftly pivoted, announcing it is 'no longer minded' to recommend a rival £6.90-per-share (£5.5bn) proposal from Castlelake. Apollo's bid represents a massive 81% premium to easyJet's share price back in late May before the takeover interest became public.

This is a textbook example of US sponsors treating London-listed mid-caps as an absolute bargain bin. UK take-privates hit £12.5bn in the first four months of 2026 alone, driven by the persistent valuation discount of the London market compared to Wall Street. For arbitrageurs and M&A desks, this is pure gold. However, Apollo faces a major regulatory headache: EU rules require airlines operating within the bloc to be majority European-owned. To get around this, Apollo is proposing an equity alternative that allows existing European shareholders to roll over their stakes.

items: What to say at work: Two bidders are always better than one. Apollo's intervention shows that despite soaring jet fuel costs and geopolitical headwinds, private equity is still hungry for unloved UK mid-caps. The real test will be how they structure the deal to satisfy EU ownership rules without forcing a messy break-up.

Interview tip: If asked about UK M&A trends, point to the easyJet battle as evidence of the 'valuation gap' between London and New York, and how PE firms are using creative structures to bypass regulatory ownership caps.

content.text: 3. Xavier Niel's 'White Swan' Vodafone Move: A £4.4bn Power Play

French telecoms billionaire Xavier Niel has pulled off a massive coup, agreeing to buy Emirates Telecommunications' (e&) entire 16.2% stake in Vodafone for £4.4bn (112.5p per share) through his investment vehicle, Vega. The deal represents a 15% premium to Vodafone's previous close and makes Niel the company's largest shareholder. Vodafone shares reacted by surging 13% on Friday, marking a dramatic shift in the company's shareholder register.

Telecoms have been a notorious value trap for a decade, but Niel is not a passive passenger. As the founder of Iliad, he is a legendary consolidator who knows how to wring cash out of legacy networks. His entry ends Vodafone's relationship agreement with e& and is expected to accelerate the group's ongoing restructuring, particularly following its UK merger with CK Hutchison and exits from Spain and Italy. However, the UK government—which previously flagged e&'s stake as a national security risk—will likely scrutinise Niel's purchase closely.

items: What to say at work: Xavier Niel buying out e& is a massive vote of confidence in Vodafone's turnaround. He's a legendary operator who doesn't do passive investing—expect him to push management hard on extracting value in Germany and the UK. It's a classic sum-of-the-parts play.

Interview tip: Use this story to discuss activist investing and corporate restructuring. Explain how a concentrated, strategic shareholder can force management to accelerate asset sales and cost-cutting measures.

content.text: 4. SK Hynix's Blockbuster US Debut: The AI Chip Boom Hits Nasdaq

South Korean memory giant SK Hynix completed its massive US listing on Nasdaq on July 10, raising $26.5 billion in one of the largest US listings of the year. Shares opened 14% above their offer price and are trading under the ticker SKHY. The company is the undisputed king of High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) chips, which are the physical bottleneck in Nvidia's AI GPUs.

For tech ECM and asset managers, this is a monumental event. Previously, investing in the physical backbone of the AI boom required navigating the complex South Korean market or buying Nvidia. The Nasdaq listing gives global capital direct, liquid access to the ultimate pick-and-shovel play of the AI era. It also sets up a fascinating valuation comparison with US rival Micron and domestic competitor Samsung.

items: What to say at work: SK Hynix listing on Nasdaq is the ultimate pick-and-shovel play for the AI trade. If you want exposure to AI but think Nvidia's valuation is too frothy, Hynix is the physical bottleneck everyone has to pay. It's a pure play on AI infrastructure.

Interview tip: When discussing AI valuations, highlight the difference between software-level AI plays (high margin, high execution risk) and hardware infrastructure plays like SK Hynix (highly cyclical, but with massive near-term pricing power due to physical supply constraints).

content.text: 5. Prologis Ramps Up the Heat on Segro: The £12.6bn Warehouse War

US logistics giant Prologis has released a fresh investor presentation ramping up pressure on FTSE 100 warehouse giant Segro to engage with its unsolicited £12.6bn (925p per share) all-share takeover bid. Segro's board has repeatedly rejected the bid as 'opportunistic' and 'undervalued,' claiming its portfolio is worth over £13 per share. Prologis is arguing that a merger would allow them to access a massive global data centre pipeline (5.8GW secured) that Segro cannot fund alone due to balance sheet constraints.

Real estate M&A is heating up. The battle highlights the premium being placed on 'digital infrastructure' (data centres) over traditional industrial sheds. In the AI era, securing gigawatts of power capacity is the new land grab. Prologis is trying to convince Segro's shareholders that its superior balance sheet and access to private capital make it the better vehicle to exploit this opportunity.

items: What to say at work: Prologis isn't just buying warehouses; they are buying power grids. The real prize here is Segro's data centre pipeline. In the AI era, securing gigawatts of power capacity is the new land grab.

Interview tip: Be ready to discuss how traditional sectors like real estate are being reshaped by the AI boom. Data centres require massive power and cooling infrastructure, making REITs with secured power allocations highly valuable acquisition targets.

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The Weekend Hangover: Geopolitics Crashes the AI Party

If Friday's market was a crisp pint of lager in a sunny City beer garden, Monday morning is the lukewarm, flat dregs left on the table after a pub brawl. On Friday, Wall Street was still riding high on the artificial intelligence boom. The S&P 500 edged up 0.4% to close at 7,575.39, while the Nasdaq added 0.3% to 26,281.61, capped off by South Korean chip giant SK Hynix pulling off a monster $26.5bn Nasdaq debut—the largest ever by a foreign firm on a US exchange—with its shares soaring 13%. But over the weekend, geopolitics did what it does best: ruined the party. The month-long US-Iran ceasefire has officially collapsed, with both sides trading airstrikes and Iran claiming it has closed the vital Strait of Hormuz. Consequently, Brent crude spiked by as much as 5% early Monday before settling around 2.3% higher at $77.72 a barrel.

The cross-asset reaction has been swift and unforgiving. In Asia, Tokyo's Nikkei 225 shed 1.9% to 67,242.73, while Seoul's Kospi got absolutely battered, plunging 9% to 6,806.93—its worst day since May. SK Hynix’s domestic shares in Seoul plummeted 15.4%, completely erasing the Nasdaq IPO euphoria, while rival Samsung Electronics sank 10.7%. US stock futures are firmly in the red, with Nasdaq futures down 0.9% and S&P 500 futures off 0.3%. European indices are barely holding flat. The message from the screens is clear: the market is terrified of a stagflationary cocktail where energy shocks collide with sticky inflation.
The Bond Market's Grim Reality Check

It's not just equities feeling the heat; the bond market is flashing warning signs. The US 10-year Treasury yield ticked up to 4.58% on Monday morning, up from Friday's close of 4.56%, while the 2-year yield remains sticky around 4.21%. Under the hood, long-term real yields (inflation-protected Treasuries) are hovering at multi-decade highs. The Fed's June minutes, released last week, revealed a deeply divided committee, and futures markets are now pricing in two rate hikes over the next 12 months. Remember when the consensus was penciling in three cuts for 2026? That trade is dead and buried. Higher oil prices feed directly into the hawkish narrative, meaning borrowers and equity bulls alike should get comfortable with higher-for-longer rates.
Warsh's New Model Army: Overhauling the Fed

The macro backdrop is complicated further by the aggressive reform agenda of the new Federal Reserve Chair, Kevin Warsh. Sworn in on May 22, Warsh has already made waves by ending the Fed's long-standing practice of explicit 'forward guidance'—essentially telling markets that the era of central bank hand-holding is over. Over the weekend, Warsh announced the formation of five independent task forces to re-examine the Fed's monetary policy framework. The advisory panels are a who's who of heavy hitters, including former Bank of England Governor Mervyn King (a vocal critic of forward guidance), former RBI Governor Raghuram Rajan, and Silicon Valley venture capitalist Marc Andreessen.

The inclusion of Andreessen is a fascinating nod to the idea that AI-driven productivity gains could be structurally deflationary, a theory Warsh seems keen to explore. However, the immediate challenge is highly cyclical. Warsh is scheduled to deliver his semi-annual Congressional testimony on Tuesday (House) and Wednesday (Senate). Expect lawmakers to grill him on whether the Fed will be forced to squeeze the brakes even harder if the Middle East conflict keeps oil prices elevated.
The Week Ahead: The Ultimate Stress Test

This week is shaping up to be the ultimate stress test for the equity market's resilience. On Tuesday, we get the June US CPI report. Headline inflation is expected to slow below 4%, but core CPI is forecast to hold sticky at 2.9%—well above the Fed's 2% target. On the very same day, the Q2 earnings season kicks off with the Wall Street behemoths: JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Citigroup all report.

Why does this matter so much? According to Goldman Sachs research, the S&P 500's 18% rally over the past 12 months has been driven entirely by earnings growth, with zero multiple expansion (the forward P/E has remained flat at 20x). This means equities have no valuation cushion. If the big banks miss expectations, or if their net interest income guidance is clouded by Warsh's unpredictable, guidance-free Fed, the market's floor could give way very quickly.

items: The SK Hynix arbitrage: The South Korean chipmaker's massive $26.5bn Nasdaq debut on Friday was a triumph, but the 15% crash in its Seoul-listed shares on Monday shows how quickly geopolitical risk can overwhelm micro fundamentals.

Warsh's Fed is a different beast: By killing forward guidance and assembling a task force featuring Mervyn King and Marc Andreessen, Kevin Warsh is actively dismantling the Bernanke-Powell communication playbook. Expect more market volatility as investors learn to live without a Fed safety net.

Earnings are the only game in town: With the forward P/E flat at 20x, the S&P 500 is entirely dependent on corporate earnings delivering. If the big banks disappoint on Tuesday, there is no valuation cushion to catch the fall.

content.text: Most junior analysts spend 90% of their time building ridiculously complex Excel models to forecast demand. They will model the exact number of electric vehicles sold in 2032, or the precise growth rate of enterprise SaaS spend. But here is the dirty secret of the buy-side: demand is incredibly hard to forecast, and even when you get it right, you can still lose your shirt. Why? Because you ignored the supply side.

This is where the Capital Cycle comes in. Popularised by the legendary London-based asset manager Marathon Asset Management (and compiled in the brilliant book Capital Returns), capital cycle theory is a supply-side framework that explains why high-performing industries eventually self-destruct, and why unloved, capital-starved sectors often become goldmines.
How the Capital Cycle Works (The Boom-to-Bust Loop)
The basic premise is beautifully simple: high returns on capital attract more capital, which eventually destroys those very returns. Here is how the loop plays out in four stages:

items: 1. The Boom: An industry is highly profitable, boasting massive Return on Invested Capital (ROIC). Think lithium mining during the EV hype, or wind turbine manufacturing, or even boutique fitness studios.

2. The Flood: Seeing these fat margins, existing players aggressively expand capacity (Capex), and venture capital or private equity funds flood the sector with cheap money. Investment banks eagerly underwrite IPOs and M&A deals.
3. The Glut: All this new capacity comes online at the same time. Suddenly, supply vastly outstrips demand. Price wars break out, margins collapse, and ROIC plummets.

4. The Purge: Companies go bust, projects are mothballed, and capital flees. The industry becomes uninvestable. But as capacity shrinks and no one reinvests, supply tightens. Eventually, demand catches up, prices rise, and the survivors enjoy a massive, highly profitable recovery.

content.text: A Simple Example: The Lithium Rollercoaster

Let us look at lithium. In the early 2020s, everyone agreed on the demand story: electric vehicles were the future, and we needed mountains of lithium. Prices skyrocketed. Mining companies, flush with cash and encouraged by Wall Street, launched massive capital expenditure programmes to dig new mines. But mines take years to build. By the time all these new mines opened, they created a massive supply glut. Lithium prices crashed by over 80% from their peak. Even though EV demand kept growing globally, lithium mining stocks got absolutely hammered because the supply grew far faster. That is the capital cycle in action.
Why This Matters in Asset Management

In asset management, understanding the capital cycle helps you avoid 'growth traps'—companies that look amazing today but are about to face a wall of industry-wide supply. Conversely, it helps you find incredible 'value' opportunities in unloved, capital-starved sectors where consolidated players have pricing power because nobody else is building competing capacity.
Common Beginner Mistake: The TAM Trap

The classic rookie error is falling in love with a massive Total Addressable Market (TAM) and high current margins, without looking at the aggregate industry Capex. If industry Capex is growing at 40% year-on-year while demand is growing at 20%, it does not matter how disruptive the product is—industry profitability is going to get shredded.
How to Use This in Interviews

If you are interviewing at a long-only asset manager or a multi-manager hedge fund, bringing up the capital cycle is an instant credibility booster. It shows you think like a business owner, not just a spreadsheet jockey. If they ask you to pitch a stock, don't just talk about why customers love it. Walk them through the supply dynamics: 'Industry-wide Capex has been depressed for five years, two major competitors recently consolidated, and there is virtually no new capacity coming online. This gives our target company massive pricing power as demand recovers.'
Over a Pint: What to Say at the Pub

Everyone in the City is obsessed with forecasting the demand side of AI chips. But the real question is whether the massive, multi-billion-pound capex boom from the big tech players is going to trigger a classic capital cycle glut in foundry capacity in a few years.

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day: Shapley-Based Portfolio Performance Contribution (SPPC)

If you have ever sat in an investment committee trying to explain why your shiny new machine learning model is positioning the fund the way it is, you have probably reached for SHAP values. You show a nice beeswarm plot, point to '12-month momentum' at the top, and hope everyone nods. But there is a massive, gaping hole in this approach: traditional SHAP tells you which features drive the model's predictions (e.g., reducing Mean Squared Error). It does not tell you which features actually drive portfolio performance (e.g., your Sharpe ratio or alpha). In the City, we do not eat R-squared; we eat risk-adjusted returns.

Enter Shapley-Based Portfolio Performance Contribution (SPPC), a framework introduced in a brilliant paper, 'The Anatomy of Machine Learning-Based Portfolio Performance', by Philippe Goulet Coulombe, David E. Rapach, Erik Christian Montes Schütte, and Sander Schwenk-Nebbe. SPPC bridges the gap between machine learning interpretability and actual economic value by applying cooperative game theory directly to the end-to-end portfolio pipeline.
The Core Concept: From Predictions to PnL

Think of your features as players in a pub quiz team. Traditional SHAP measures who shouted out the most answers (predictive impact). SPPC measures who actually got the high-scoring questions right that won you the fifty-pound bar tab (portfolio performance). To calculate SPPC, you do not just look at the model's output. You run the entire pipeline—prediction, portfolio construction (e.g., sorting stocks into long-short quintiles), and performance evaluation (e.g., calculating the Sharpe ratio)—for every possible combination of feature subsets. You then use Shapley values to fairly allocate the final Sharpe ratio among the features.
A Quick Python-ish Look

Here is a conceptual sketch of how you would calculate the SPPC of a specific feature (like 'value') in a toy three-feature setup. In practice, you would group features to avoid the combinatorial explosion.

import itertools
import numpy as np

features = ['momentum', 'value', 'volatility']

def evaluate_portfolio_sharpe(feature_subset):
    if not feature_subset:
        return 0.0
    # 1. Train model on subset
    # 2. Generate out-of-sample forecasts
    # 3. Construct long-short portfolio
    # 4. Return the Sharpe ratio
    return run_pipeline(feature_subset)

# Compute SPPC for 'value'
target = 'value'
other_features = [f for f in features if f != target]
sppc_value = 0.0

for r in range(len(other_features) + 1):
    for subset in itertools.combinations(other_features, r):
        subset = list(subset)
        # Sharpe with the target feature
        sharpe_with = evaluate_portfolio_sharpe(subset + [target])
        # Sharpe without the target feature
        sharpe_without = evaluate_portfolio_sharpe(subset)
        
        # Weight based on Shapley formula
        weight = np.math.factorial(len(subset)) * np.math.factorial(len(features) - len(subset) - 1) / np.math.factorial(len(features))
        sppc_value += weight * (sharpe_with - sharpe_without)

print(f"Value's contribution to the portfolio Sharpe: {sppc_value:.2f}")
Why This Matters for Interviews and Work

items: The PM Conversation: Next time a PM asks, 'Why is this model making us money?', do not show them a feature importance plot of MSE. Use SPPC to say: 'Our momentum signals contributed 0.8 to our 1.5 Sharpe ratio, but our value signals actually dragged it down by 0.2 once transaction costs were factored in.' That is music to a PM's ears.

The Interview Edge: If you are asked how to evaluate feature importance in a quantitative trading strategy, do not just regurgitate 'random forest feature importance' or 'permutation importance.' Explain that these are decision-blind. Pivot to SPPC: explain how you can wrap the entire portfolio optimization and transaction cost model inside a Shapley framework to attribute the Sharpe ratio itself. It shows you think like a commercial risk-taker, not just a Kaggle competitor.

content.text: The Catch

The obvious elephant in the room is computational cost. If you have 200 features, calculating two-to-the-power-of-two-hundred model training and portfolio simulation runs will melt your firm's cloud budget before lunch. To make this practical, the authors suggest grouping features into a few thematic 'coalitions' (e.g., grouping 200 features into 5 categories: Momentum, Value, Quality, Size, and Risk). This reduces the problem to thirty-two evaluations, which is easily doable on a standard workstation.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: If you’ve spent any time in a City meeting room recently, you’ve probably had some bright spark show you a backtest of an LLM-based trading strategy boasting a Sharpe ratio that would make Jim Simons blush. Before you hand over your capital (or your career), you need to read a brilliant position paper from a team of quant and AI heavyweights, including Alejandro Lopez-Lira and Oxford’s Stefan Zohren.

The paper is called "Evaluating LLMs in Finance Requires Explicit Bias Consideration" (arXiv:2602.14233). It is a systematic, cold-water-to-the-face review of how we evaluate AI in finance. The authors reviewed 164 academic papers on financial LLMs published between 2023 and 2025, and the results are, frankly, terrifying. They found that the academic and vendor communities are routinely committing what they call the "Five Sins" of financial LLM evaluation, creating a massive "illusion of validity."
The Five Sins of Financial LLM Evaluation

items: Sin #1: Look-Ahead Bias (The Time-Traveler): LLMs are trained on historical data. If you ask GPT-4 (trained up to late 2023) to "predict" stock moves in early 2023, it isn't predicting; it's remembering. Yet, only 26.8% of the 164 papers reviewed even acknowledged this. If the model's weights already contain the future, your backtest is just a memory test.

Sin #2: Survivorship Bias (The Ghost Hunter): Only 1.2% of the reviewed papers accounted for this. If you only evaluate your LLM on companies that are active today (e.g., the current S&P 500), you ignore all the firms that went bust along the way. Your AI looks like a genius simply because it never had the chance to buy Enron.

Sin #3: Narrative Bias (The Bullsh*tter): LLMs are designed to write beautiful, highly plausible stories. In finance, this is dangerous. A model can generate an incredibly convincing narrative for why a stock will rise, masking a complete lack of statistical edge or risk-adjusted reality. It creates an "illusion of understanding."

Sin #4: Objective Bias (The Confident Guesser): Standard LLMs are fine-tuned (via RLHF) to be helpful and always provide an answer. In the real world, the most valuable skill a trader or analyst has is knowing when to say "I don't know" and sit on their hands. LLMs are structurally biased to hallucinate certainty rather than abstain.

Sin #5: Cost Bias (The Paper Millionaire): Many papers show "profitable" strategies while completely ignoring transaction fees, bid-ask spreads, borrow costs, and the actual API/compute costs of running the model. A strategy with a tiny edge that trades 100 times a day will bleed to death in the real world once you add 5 bps of slippage and a hefty OpenAI bill.

content.text: Why This Matters to You

Whether you are a quant developer, an asset management analyst, or an investment banker, LLMs are creeping into your workflow. If you are interviewing, being able to talk about the structural flaws of financial LLMs—rather than just parroting the hype—instantly marks you out as a serious practitioner who understands market reality.
What to Skim

Skip the heavy machine learning architecture details in the middle. Instead, focus on Section 2 (which details the "Five Sins" with concrete examples) and Section 3, where they introduce their "Structural Validity Framework"—essentially a checklist for how to build a backtest that isn't complete fiction.
What to Say Over a Pint

The next time someone shows you an LLM-driven trading model, don't ask about the returns. Ask them: 'How did you temporally sanitize the training data to prevent look-ahead bias, and what was your active universe construction to avoid survivorship bias?' Watch them sweat.
Our Take

This paper is a public service. The financial industry has a long history of dressing up old statistical errors in shiny new clothes, and "AI-driven investing" is the latest runway model. By formalising these biases, the authors have given us a toolkit to separate genuine alpha from expensive noise. If you are building or buying financial AI, this is your new bible.

sources.title: Evaluating LLMs in Finance Requires Explicit Bias Consideration

content.text: The "But You Are Free" Technique

Imagine you are trying to get a senior portfolio manager to look at a new risk model you have built, or you are trying to coax a client into a follow-up meeting. Your natural instinct is to pitch hard, sell the benefits, and make the next step feel inevitable. But human psychology has a built-in defense mechanism called psychological reactance. The moment people feel their autonomy is being squeezed—even slightly—their subconscious pushes back just to regain control.

This is where a beautifully simple piece of behavioral science comes in: the "But You Are Free" (BYAF) technique. First demonstrated by French psychologists Nicolas Guéguen and Alexandre Pascual in 2000, and later backed by a massive meta-analysis of 42 studies by Christopher Carpenter in 2013, the concept is almost laughably simple. If you make a request and immediately follow it up by explicitly acknowledging the other person's freedom to refuse, your compliance rates can literally double.

In the original French study, researchers went around asking passersby for spare change for the bus. When they just asked for money, only 10% complied. But when they added, "but you are free to accept or refuse," the compliance rate jumped to 47.5%, and those who did give gave twice as much. By explicitly giving people an "out," you disarm their psychological defenses. They no longer feel manipulated or cornered, so they can evaluate your request on its merits rather than fighting for their cognitive independence.
How to use it in the City: This is not about being passive-aggressive or sounding like a wet weekend. It is about strategic deference. You can use this in emails, pitches, or when managing upwards:

items: When pitching a client: "We would love to walk you through our new mid-cap strategy next Tuesday. Obviously, it is entirely up to you if you have the capacity right now, but let me know if that works."
When asking a colleague for a favour: "Could you cast an eye over these slides before the committee meeting? No pressure at all if you are slammed, completely your call."
When managing upwards: "I have drafted two options for the restructuring plan. I think Option A is the strongest route, but of course, the final decision is entirely yours."

content.text: The exact phrasing does not matter—"it is your call," "no pressure," "completely up to you" all work. The magic lies in the direct interaction. By handing them the steering wheel, you make it safe for them to agree with you.
To get people to say yes, remind them they have the power to say no.
